draft.title: Designing a program for an athlete
card: A program starts with an activity analysis. This lists the energy systems, fitness components and movements the sport demands, so training matches the sport.
Fitness test results show the athlete's strengths and weaknesses. Training time goes to the areas that most limit performance in that sport.
The training principles shape the plan. Specificity matches training to the sport, progressive overload raises the load over time, and variety and recovery help the athlete cope with the work.
A program is not fixed. Retesting shows how the athlete has improved, and the program is changed to suit the new results.
draft.remember: Analyse the sport, test the athlete, apply the principles, then retest and adjust.

a.q: Why does a coach retest an athlete part way through a program?
opts: To see what has changed and adjust the program
To check the activity analysis was written correctly
To show the athlete the principles no longer apply
To keep the same program for the whole season
a.why: Retesting shows how the athlete has improved, so the coach can change the program to suit the new results. It does not replace the activity analysis or remove the training principles, and the program is not meant to stay fixed.
a.clue: Think about what the results show after weeks of training.

b.q: Ayesha plays netball in Geelong. Her tests show good aerobic fitness but slow repeated sprints, and her sport needs short, fast efforts. What is the best way to build her program?
opts: Add repeated sprint work, then increase the load over time
Add long steady runs, as her results show aerobic fitness
Copy the program of a marathon runner with the same age
Train all fitness components equally for the whole season
b.why: The activity analysis shows netball needs short, fast efforts, and her tests show repeated sprints are the weakness. Training time goes there, with progressive overload as she improves. Long steady runs build a strength she already has and do not match the sport.
b.clue: Match the weak result to what the sport demands.

a.best: To see what has changed and adjust the program

b.best: Add repeated sprint work, then increase the load over time

problems.detail: Recovery is presented as a training principle, but it is not one of the training principles named in the VCE PE Study Design (frequency, intensity, time, type, progression, specificity, individuality, diminishing returns, variety, maintenance, overtraining, detraining). The card also says variety helps the athlete 'cope with the work', when its main role is reducing boredom and keeping motivation. Reword it, for example: 'variety keeps training interesting, and enough rest helps avoid overtraining.'
The option 'Copy the program of a marathon runner with the same age' is awkwardly worded. It should read 'of the same age'.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer, and the explanations match the card. The card lists 'recovery' as a training principle, which it is not in the VCE Study Design. One distractor in question b also has a small grammar slip.
